===== Investigation: PSI-69 =====

[i_Investigation.txt p.1]
Study Identifier	PSI-69
Study Title	Flame Extinguishment Experiment
Study Submission Date	31-Jul-2016
Study Public Release Date	31-Jul-2016
Comment[Approach]	The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .
The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows:
1. Select the test pressure (0.5 - 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests.
2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm)
3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size).
4. Perform a droplet combustion test.
5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed).
6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction).
7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction.
8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite.
There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI . For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow. In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed).
The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity. Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.
Comment[DOI]	10.60555/mbq8-0451
Comment[Experiment Hardware]	Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)-Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)
Comment[Flight Platform]	International Space Station (ISS)
Comment[Funding]	NNX09AM33A
Comment[Hypothesis]	The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.
Comment[Investigation Acronym]	FLEX
Comment[Investigation End Date]	07-31-2016
Comment[Investigation Start Date]	08-01-2007
Comment[Managing NASA Center]	Glenn Research Center (GRC)
Comment[Objective]	The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
Comment[Project Type]	Microgravity Investigation
Comment[Proposal Title]	Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity
Comment[Research Area]	Combustion Science
Comment[Research Impacts]	The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.
Comment[Space Program]	National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
Comment[SubResearch Area]	Spacecraft Fire Safety
Study Design Type	FLEX Fuel Sooting Droplet Spacecraft Fire Safety Diffusion Flames Flames


===== Investigation: PSI-99 =====

[i_Investigation.txt p.1]
Study Identifier	PSI-99
Study Title	Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II
Study Submission Date	18-Sep-2024
Study Public Release Date	18-Sep-2024
Comment[Approach]	The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science's Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm. Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.
Comment[DOI]	10.60555/2chp-m469
Comment[Experiment Hardware]	Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module, SAFFIRE
Comment[Flight Platform]	Cygnus Spacecraft
Comment[Funding]	NASA
Comment[Hypothesis]	This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
Comment[Investigation Acronym]	SAFFIRE-II
Comment[Investigation End Date]	04-01-2017
Comment[Investigation Start Date]	09-30-2016
Comment[Managing NASA Center]	Glenn Research Center (GRC)
Comment[Objective]	The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA's normal gravity material flammability screening test.
Comment[Project Type]	Microgravity Investigation
Comment[Research Area]	Combustion Science
Comment[Research Impacts]	The Saffire-II experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA's material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.
Comment[Space Program]	National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
Comment[SubResearch Area]	Surface Combustion
Study Design Type	fire fire safety Cygnus Nomex SAFFIRE SHS Smoldering Smoke Distribution
Comment[orcidIdentifier]	0000-0002-7397-2033

===== Investigation: PSI-102 =====

[i_Investigation.txt p.1]
Study Identifier	PSI-102
Study Title	Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
Study Submission Date	18-Sep-2024
Study Public Release Date	18-Sep-2024
Comment[Approach]	The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.
Comment[DOI]	10.60555/gd4k-8h62
Comment[Experiment Hardware]	Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware
Comment[Flight Platform]	International Space Station (ISS)
Comment[Funding]	IH1013215
Comment[Hypothesis]	The three hypotheses that motivated this investigation:
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.
Comment[Investigation Acronym]	SAME
Comment[Investigation End Date]	02-28-2008
Comment[Investigation Start Date]	03-02-2001
Comment[Managing NASA Center]	Glenn Research Center (GRC)
Comment[Objective]	One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
Comment[Project Type]	Microgravity Investigation
Comment[Research Area]	Combustion Science
Comment[Research Impacts]	The SAME experiment will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.
Comment[Space Program]	National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
Comment[SubResearch Area]	Spacecraft Fire Safety
Study Design Type	Smoke Bio-Astronautics Surface Combustion Smoldering Fire Safety
